title: Molinaeus: justification from eternity — faith gives the sense of it
source_text: LXXI. Nec videtur ab hac sententia alienus Petrus Molinaeus, saepius jam citatus, & Theologiae in Academia Sedanensi Professor. Hic enim justificationem censet esse ab aeterno, & in eo differre a regeneratione, quae fit in tempore, & habet initium. Nam loquens de justificatione hominis coram Deo, Illa, inquit, est ab aeterno & ante saecula, quippe pars decreti electionis, quamvis ejus sensus detur fidelibus certo tempore. At haec nempe regeneratio, fit in tempore, & habet quoddam initium, nempe primas scintillas fidei, & primulos motus poenitentiae. De Justificatione & Fide justificante, part. 1. Thesi 54. Proinde, ex ejus hypothesi, peccatori peccata remissa sunt antequam credat, nec aliter fides justificat, quam quia per fidem habemus justificationis sensum.
pass_a_gloss: Nor does Peter du Moulin, already often cited, and Professor of Theology in the Academy of Sedan, seem foreign to this opinion. For he judges justification to be from eternity, and in that to differ from regeneration, which is done in time and has a beginning. For speaking of the justification of a man before God, That, he says, is from eternity and before the ages, inasmuch as it is part of the decree of election, although the sense of it is given to the faithful at a certain time. But this, namely regeneration, is done in time, and has a certain beginning, namely the first sparks of faith and the first little motions of repentance. On Justification and Justifying Faith, part 1, Thesis 54. Accordingly, from his hypothesis, sins have been remitted to the sinner before he believes, nor does faith justify otherwise than because through faith we have the sense of justification.
pass_b_english: Du Moulin (Sedan): justification is from eternity — part of the election decree — unlike regeneration, which begins in time.
Sense of justification is given to believers at a certain time; regeneration’s start is first sparks of faith and first motions of repentance.
On his hypothesis: sins remitted before the sinner believes.
Faith justifies only inasmuch as through faith we have the sense of justification.
